justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current price level for the underlying asset (likely SPY or a similar broad equity index trading around 540). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a slight upward bias, reflecting the typical mean-reverting tendency of daily returns and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts I could identify with high confidence. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher, incorporating a small positive equity risk premium over time while acknowledging that a week is long enough for meaningful price discovery. At the one-month horizon, I applied a somewhat larger drift upward, consistent with the historical long-run tendency of equities to appreciate, though the magnitude remains conservative given the uncertainty inherent in a 30-day window.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each respective horizon. Daily realized volatility for large-cap equity indices has typically run in the range of 0.8–1.2% on an annualized basis expressed daily, so a roughly plus-or-minus 14-point band at one day felt appropriate. As I extended to one week, I widened the interval to reflect the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility as well as the increased probability of encountering macro data releases, Fed communications, or geopolitical developments. The one-month interval was widened further still, capturing the reality that a month contains multiple potential inflection points including earnings seasons, central bank meetings, and economic releases that compound uncertainty substantially.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden deterioration in credit markets or banking stress, an unexpected inflation print that reprices Federal Reserve policy expectations dramatically, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict that triggers risk-off positioning globally. On the upside, a surprisingly strong labor market or consumer spending report combined with dovish Fed guidance could propel prices well above the upper bound of even my one-month interval. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets around holidays or unexpected institutional repositioning can produce gap moves that my intervals, which assume roughly normal return distributions, would underestimate.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry meaningful model uncertainty in addition to market uncertainty. My intervals assume something close to log-normal return dynamics with stationary volatility, but volatility clustering means that if we are entering a high-volatility regime, my bands could be far too narrow. Conversely, if conditions are unusually calm, realized outcomes might cluster tightly around my point estimates. Tail events — flash crashes, circuit breakers, or extraordinary policy interventions — are by their nature underweighted in any probabilistic framework built on recent historical patterns.
